The guideline values for 1,2-dichlorobenzene (1,2-DCB) and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (1,4-DCB) in drinking water are significantly higher than their lowest reported taste thresholds, which are 1 µg/L and 6 µg/L, respectively. This indicates that these compounds can be detected by taste at much lower concentrations than the guideline values. 2. No health-based guideline value has been established for 1,3-dichlorobenzene due to insufficient data to derive such a value. The assessment was conducted in 1993, with the principal reference being the WHO (2003) report on dichlorobenzenes in drinking water. 3. 1,1-Dichloroethane is used as a chemical intermediate and solvent. It has been detected in drinking water at concentrations up to 10 µg/L, primarily in groundwater. However, no health-based guideline value has been established due to limited toxicity data. It is rapidly metabolized in mammals to acetic acid and chlorinated compounds, with relatively low acute toxicity. Limited evidence exists for genotoxicity, and one carcinogenicity study in mice and rats showed no conclusive evidence of carcinogenicity, though there was some indication of increased hemangiosarcomas in treated animals. 4. 1,2-Dichloroethane is primarily used as an intermediate in the production of vinyl chloride and other chemicals, and to a lesser extent as a solvent. It can enter surface waters through industrial effluents and persist in groundwater for long periods. It has been classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) due to evidence of tumor formation in laboratory animals. Toxicity targets include the immune system, central nervous system, liver, and kidneys. It is less potent when inhaled compared to oral exposure. 5. 1,1-Dichloroethene, also known as vinylidene chloride, is used as a monomer in the production of polyvinylidene chloride copolymers and as an intermediate in organic chemical synthesis. It is occasionally found in drinking water, often alongside other chlorinated hydrocarbons. It is a central nervous system depressant and may cause liver and kidney toxicity in humans exposed occupationally. IARC has classified it as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans). It has shown genotoxicity in vitro but not in vivo. Kidney tumors were observed in mice in one inhalation study, but other studies, including those using drinking water, did not find evidence of carcinogenicity. 6. 1,2-Dichloroethene exists in cis and trans isomeric forms, with the cis form more commonly found as a water contaminant. Both isomers are metabolites of other unsaturated halogenated hydrocarbons. The trans isomer has been associated with reduced kidney weights in rats at higher doses, while the cis isomer is metabolized more rapidly. Both isomers have shown some genotoxic activity, but no information is available on their carcinogenicity. The presence of these isomers in groundwater may indicate the presence of other organochlorine chemicals, such as vinyl chloride, necessitating more intensive monitoring. 7. Dichloromethane, or methylene chloride, is widely used as a solvent for various purposes, including coffee decaffeination and paint stripping. Exposure from drinking water is likely insignificant compared to other sources. It has low acute toxicity, and inhalation studies in mice provided conclusive evidence of carcinogenicity, while drinking water studies in rats and mice provided only suggestive evidence. IARC has classified it as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), but the balance of evidence suggests it is not a genotoxic carcinogen. 8. 1,2-Dichloropropane (1,2-DCP) is used as an insecticide fumigant and as an intermediate in the production of chlorinated products. It has been classified by IARC as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans) due to limited evidence of carcinogenicity in experimental animals and insufficient data in humans. Mutagenicity assays have shown mixed results, and in vivo studies were negative. A threshold approach for toxicological evaluation was deemed appropriate. 9. 1,3-Dichloropropane is rarely found in water and is of low acute toxicity. There is some indication of genotoxicity in bacterial systems, but no short-term, long-term, reproductive, or developmental toxicity data relevant to drinking water exposure are available. The data are insufficient to recommend a guideline value. 10. 1,3-Dichloropropene is a soil fumigant used to control soil pests, particularly nematodes. It is soluble in water and can be a potential water contaminant. It is a direct-acting mutagen and has been shown to produce tumors in the forestomach, bladder, lungs, and liver of laboratory animals following long-term exposure. IARC has classified it as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans). 11. Chlorophenoxy herbicides, including dichlorprop, have been classified by IARC as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans). However, available data do not permit an assessment of the carcinogenic potential of specific chlorophenoxy herbicides. Drinking water guidelines are based on a threshold approach for other toxic effects, such as renal toxicity observed in long-term dietary studies in rats. 12. Dichlorvos is an organophosphorus insecticide used for controlling household pests and protecting stored products. It is no longer approved in some jurisdictions due to concerns over acute toxicity. It is rapidly degraded in soil and water and does not adsorb to sediments. Cholinesterase inhibition, causing neurotoxicity, is the most sensitive toxicological endpoint. Dichlorvos is unlikely to be genotoxic in vivo or pose a carcinogenic risk to humans. Some reproductive toxicity has been observed in rats, but it is not teratogenic. 13. Dicofol is an organochlorine acaricide used to control plant-eating mites. It is soluble in water and can be removed by reverse osmosis with high efficiency. Conventional water treatment methods are not effective. Dicofol has been classified as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) by IARC.
